meta.description: Discover what living in Panama is like: cost of living, transport, healthcare, education, safety, nature and the differences between the capital and the interior.

healthcare.title: Healthcare System
healthcare.subtitle: Health & Wellbeing
healthcare.shortDescription: In line with Panamanian legislation, every citizen has the inalienable right to medical care. The country operates a dual public-private system with modern facilities and internationally trained physicians.

sections.body:
In line with Panamanian legislation, every citizen has the inalienable right to medical care, and the public healthcare system theoretically works for all. This service, offered in various health centers, usually comes at a low cost, although it's free for children under five years old.

Health centers are established in all urban municipalities, and despite the Pan American Health Organization noting a lesser presence in rural areas, access to care remains relatively uniform. However, the quality of care, especially for specialties, varies greatly across the country. This public system operates alongside a well-established private healthcare system.

sections.heading: Public Healthcare System
sections.body:
The Panamanian public healthcare system is managed by two entities. Firstly, the Ministry of Health (MINSA), which ensures equity and quality, coordinates assistance in Health Centers, including for foreigners. Secondly, the Social Security Fund (CSS) regulates work-related and pension insurances and provides access to maternity and illness services in its health centers spread across the country.

While not free, healthcare services remain accessible to the majority of the population, both nationals and foreigners. A contribution system through employment exists, but specialized staff intervene to adjust payment modalities when solvency is lacking, ensuring continuity of care even in financial difficulty. Panama has made significant progress in healthcare over the last twenty years, focusing on improving quality and access. The system is often cited as one of the best in Central America, although disparities exist between urban and rural areas in terms of availability and quality of care.

sections.heading: Private Healthcare System
sections.body:
Alongside the public system, Panama has renowned clinics and private practices in major cities, generally considered of higher quality. In addition to the attention and quality of services, private clinics have better infrastructure, and it is easier and faster to receive treatment in this system. In Panama City, Colón, or David, you will often find English-speaking doctors trained at top international universities.

The services offered by these establishments are accessible by paying directly or are reimbursed, in whole or in part, by private health insurance or supplementary health insurance. Although only 10% of Panamanians have such insurance, many expatriates opt for this route. Most French-speaking emigrants or expatriates choose supplementary health insurance from their home country that is compatible. However, if you plan to settle in the country permanently, it is advisable to inquire about local insurance, which often offers more advantageous rates and better coverage.

meta.title: Healthcare in Panama 2026 — Public & Private System Guide
meta.description: Explore Panama's dual public-private healthcare system. Modern hospitals, internationally trained doctors, and affordable private insurance options.

economic-stability.title: Economic Stability
economic-stability.subtitle: Strategic Hub
economic-stability.shortDescription: In 1914, Panama completed the inauguration of its prestigious canal. Since then, the country has built a diversified, resilient economy that stands as a model of success in Latin America.

sections.body: In 1914, Panama completed a monumental feat with the inauguration of its prestigious canal — a dream started by Ferdinand de Lesseps in 1881. The iconic canal is more than an engineering marvel; it has catalyzed Panama's economic stability, attracting global investors. It revolutionized global transport by shortening distances and reducing costs between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.

sections.heading: Strategic Geographical Position and Economic Diversity
sections.body:
Located at the crossroads of the world, Panama has capitalized on its unique location. It's known not only for its canal but also for its thriving logistics and port sector. The creation of the International Banking Center in 1970 marked the emergence of a flourishing financial sector that continues to attract banks and investors, contributing to GDP growth.

Panama hasn't put all its eggs in one basket. Beyond the canal and free zones, the country has diversified its economy, developing sectors like tourism, finance, real estate, agriculture, and services. This diversification has reinforced its resilience to global economic turbulence.

sections.heading: Impact of Panama's Relationship with the United States
sections.body:
Panama's economic history is also marked by its close ties with the United States. The military dictatorship of Omar Torrijos Herrera in 1968, nationalist reforms, and the Torrijos-Carter Treaty of 1977 were key in shaping Panama's economic identity. Adopting the US dollar as the official currency has ensured monetary stability and simplified international transactions.

The end of the US military presence in 1999 and the return of full control of the canal marked a turning point in Panama's history. This step led to enhanced independence and unprecedented economic modernization.

sections.heading: A Model of Success in Latin America
sections.body:
Today, Panama stands out as a beacon of economic success in Latin America. Its impressive over 10% GDP growth in 2022 is a testament to its vitality. Despite challenges posed by the Covid-19 crisis, Panama continues to be a prime destination for entrepreneurs and investors worldwide.

In summary, Panama has established itself as a major player in the global economy. Its stability, diversification, special relationship with the United States, and strategic position make it a unique hub for trade, investment, and innovation. Panama is more than a country with a famous canal; it's an attractive business destination and an economic success story for every entrepreneur to consider.

meta.title: Panama's Economic Stability — Growth, Investment & Dollarization
meta.description: Learn why Panama is Latin America's economic success story. Dollarized economy, strong GDP growth, strategic canal position, and investment-friendly climate.

welcoming-country.title: Investment Opportunities
welcoming-country.subtitle: Dynamic & Welcoming
welcoming-country.shortDescription: Logistics, tourism, real estate, financial services, energy, telecoms and agribusiness: a guide to the sectors, permits, costs and steps to consider before investing in Panama.

sections.body:
Panama offers investment opportunities in logistics, tourism, real estate, financial services, energy, telecommunications and agribusiness. Two data points help to get oriented: in 2025, 2,244,078 visitors arrived through Tocumen International Airport, according to Panama Tourism Authority (ATP) statistics, and the Directorate General of Revenue (DGI) states that, in general, income tax applies to income derived from activities carried out in Panama, regardless of the nationality or residence of the beneficiary.

There is no single minimum amount, total cost or timeline for investing: they depend on the sector, the project, the permits and the applicable regime. The PROPANAMA guide states that foreign investors and their companies have the same rights and obligations as nationals. Investing does not, by itself, require applying for residency; these are separate decisions and should be assessed separately.

sections.heading: Why can Panama be attractive for investing?
sections.body:
Panama's offer combines a strategic location, international trade connections, logistics infrastructure and a services market oriented to the region. The Canal, the ports, the free zones, Tocumen airport and the land connections allow companies from different sectors to consider the country as a base for operations, distribution or service provision.

One of the advantages companies often consider is the territorial tax system. According to the DGI, taxable income includes income from activities carried out in Panama. This does not mean that all income earned abroad is automatically exempt in every situation: the source of the income and the nature of the operations must be analyzed under the Fiscal Code and the applicable special rules. A Panamanian tax advisor can review your specific structure before you invest.

Special regimes also exist for certain activities or types of company. PROPANAMA's investment regimes page describes options such as Panamá Pacífico and EMMA, among others. Each regime has activity, licensing and compliance requirements; simply incorporating a company is not enough to access its benefits.

sections.heading: Which sectors offer opportunities for investors?
sections.body:
Logistics and port infrastructure

Panama's geographic position and its maritime and air connectivity support opportunities in warehousing, transport, distribution, port services, cold chain and regional trade solutions. The Colón Free Zone presents itself as a multimodal redistribution hub for Latin America and the Caribbean.

The opportunity is not limited to building infrastructure. It can also include inventory-management technology, value-added services, specialized transport and solutions that improve supply-chain efficiency. Before entering, study the competition, operating costs, location and the actual demand from customers.

Real estate and tourism

Tourism creates opportunities in accommodation, hotel management, transport, cultural experiences, ecotourism, gastronomy and event services. In real estate, projects can cover housing, commercial premises, hotels, mixed-use properties or lodging linked to tourism activities. The potential varies widely by location and business model.

Before buying land or a property, it is essential to verify the title, land use, building permits, access to utilities and environmental restrictions. An attractive location does not by itself guarantee occupancy or profitability.

Financial services and fintech

Panama's banking center and professional-services ecosystem offer opportunities in financial technology, payment processing, compliance, business solutions and regional services. Financial activity, however, is regulated: the type of service will determine which licenses, registrations and controls are needed.

For that reason, a fintech company should first define what product it will offer, where its customers will be and how it will handle payments and data. The Superintendency of Banks of Panama and the other competent authorities are the references for identifying the rules applicable to each activity. The sector should not be presented as a promise of high returns: the potential depends on the model, the regulation, the costs and the ability to win customers.

Renewable energy

Solar, wind, hydroelectric and other clean sources may interest investors in generation, equipment, storage, efficiency and technical services. Panama has specific rules and incentives for certain activities: the Panama Energy Information System compiles the legal framework, including Law 37 of 2013 on solar plants and installations.

Incentives are not automatic. Project eligibility, licenses, environmental authorizations and applicable technical requirements must be confirmed. The assessment should also consider grid connection, land availability and the feasibility of selling or using the energy produced.

Telecommunications and data centers

International connectivity makes Panama a candidate to consider for digital infrastructure, data centers and telecommunications services. For this type of project, connectivity is only one factor: continuity of power supply, security, water availability and location also matter. Providing telecommunications services may require ASEP authorizations, so the investment plan should include regulatory and technical review from the start.

Agribusiness and food

The country's different regions and climates allow projects in the production, processing, storage, packaging and export of agricultural products and food. MIDA identifies coffee, cocoa, fruit, vegetables and other items as strategic lines for agribusiness development.

There are also opportunities in activities that connect production with the market: collection centers, irrigation systems, cold chain, food processing and innovation. PROPANAMA details some of these areas in its information on the food hub. The assessment must include water access, logistics, labor availability, health and safety, seasonality and export requirements.

sections.heading: What conditions, costs and timelines should you expect?
sections.body:
There is no general investment fee or single official timeline that applies to all projects. The table summarizes the elements that usually require analysis; specific costs must be confirmed with the relevant authorities, suppliers and advisors.

AspectWhat to reviewCosts and timelines
Incorporation and business structureType of company, activity, partners and registration obligationsVary depending on the structure and professional services
Sector licensesRequirements of ASEP, financial authorities or other bodiesDepend on the activity; may require files and evaluations
Land-use and construction permitsLand use, titles, municipal and construction permitsDepend on the location and scope of the project
Environmental assessmentWhether the project requires an environmental study or authorizationProcedure and cost depend on the category and the studies required
Incentive regimeEligibility for special zones or other regimesRequires meeting specific legal and operational conditions
Immigration residencyOnly if the investor wants to live in Panama and meets an immigration categoryA separate procedure, with its own requirements and fees

PROPANAMA's investment regimes window is a good starting point to identify options. For tax obligations, consult the DGI; for residency matters, review the current requirements of the National Immigration Service. Panama Contact supports you through all of these procedures.

sections.heading: What are the steps to evaluate an investment?
sections.body:
1. Define the business model. Specify what product or service you will offer, who your customers will be and whether you will operate locally, export or provide regional services.

  2. Study demand and competition. Use official statistics, sector data and your own studies. Distinguish between a promoted opportunity and proven commercial demand.

  3. Choose the structure and review the tax framework. Analyze whether a local company or a special regime fits the project. Confirm with the DGI how the source of the income would be determined.

  4. Verify permits and location before committing capital. Review the property title, land use, sector licenses, environmental requirements and access to essential services.

  5. Prepare a complete budget. Include purchase or rental, fit-out, permits, staff, insurance, taxes, advisory fees, working capital and compliance costs.

  6. Request formal confirmations. Ask the competent authorities about licenses and incentives. Do not base the decision solely on commercial information or on the expectation of obtaining tax benefits.

  7. Decide separately whether you need residency. A business investment and permission to live in Panama are different matters. If you want to live in the country, check the immigration category that applies to your situation.

sections.heading: What mistakes do investors often make?
sections.body:
• Assuming that investing automatically grants residency. Residency depends on an immigration category and its specific requirements.

  • Taking for granted that foreign income is never taxed. The DGI applies source criteria and tax rules that must be reviewed against the actual operations.

  • Counting on an incentive before confirming eligibility. The benefits of a special regime are conditional on legal and activity requirements.

  • Buying a property without thoroughly verifying it. The title, permitted use, permits and environmental restrictions must be reviewed before closing the transaction.

  • Confusing sector growth with guaranteed profitability. A figure for visitors, connectivity or output is no substitute for an analysis of demand, costs, risks and competition.

  • Underestimating regulatory timelines and costs. Authorizations depend on the sector, the place and the documentation; there is no universal timeline that guarantees the business will open.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions from investors
sections.body:
Can a foreigner invest in Panama?

Yes. PROPANAMA states that foreign investors and their companies have, by law, the same rights and obligations as nationals. The chosen activity may be subject to sector licenses and requirements.

Is it mandatory to obtain residency in order to invest?

Not necessarily. Investment and residency are separate procedures. A person can take part in an investment without that automatically meaning they have the right to reside in the country.

Does Panama tax income earned outside the country?

The DGI describes a system based on the source of income. Treatment depends on where and how the activities are carried out, as well as on the special rules that apply. Tax advice is recommended for each structure.

How much minimum capital do I need?

There is no single figure for all sectors. The capital required depends on the business model and on particular requirements for licenses, facilities or special regimes.

How long does it take to set up a company?

There is no general timeline that applies to all projects. Incorporation, permits, works and sector authorizations each have different schedules; the complexity of the project can lengthen the process.

Which incentive regime should I choose?

It depends on the activity, the location and the legal requirements. Review the regimes available at PROPANAMA and confirm directly with the relevant authority before structuring the project.

Which sectors should be analyzed first?

Logistics, tourism, real estate, finance and fintech, renewable energy, telecommunications and agribusiness are areas with relevant activity and institutional frameworks. Priority should be decided with market data and your own financial assessment.

Where can I verify the official information?

For investment and special regimes, consult PROPANAMA. For taxes, consult the DGI; for tourism, the ATP; for energy, the National Energy Secretariat; and for sector permits, the relevant regulatory body.

The opportunities described help guide your research, but they do not constitute financial advice or a guarantee of return. Before investing, validate the data, the applicable regime, the permits, the costs and the tax obligations for your specific project.

meta.title: Investment Opportunities in Panama 2026 — Foreign Investor Guide
meta.description: Panama investment guide: sectors with opportunities, territorial tax system, permits, costs and the steps to evaluate a project before you invest.

financial-hub.title: International Financial Hub
financial-hub.subtitle: Global Finance
financial-hub.shortDescription: Panama's financial system is undergoing significant changes, aligning with global trends through technological advancements — keeping it in a strong position in the international financial arena.

sections.body:
Panama's financial system is undergoing significant changes, aligning with global trends. These changes are driven by technological advancements and the unique characteristics of the country's financial system. Regulators and key players agree that modernization is essential to enhance competitiveness and transparency.

The combination of robust regulation, a well-developed financial structure, and the integration of advanced technologies keeps Panama in a strong position in the international financial arena. Embracing new technologies and recognizing the need to change not just technology but also processes ensures that Panama remains a robust and dynamic financial center in the region.

sections.heading: Characteristics of the Panamanian Financial System
sections.body:
The Panamanian economy is characterized by its banking monetary system, using the US dollar as the common currency. It operates without a central bank and is heavily connected to the global economy. The financial system structure includes banks, securities firms, pension funds, insurance companies, and cooperatives, accounting for 7.31% of GDP in 2021, with total assets amounting to $148,218 million.

Panama's international banking center operates as an intermediary system without a last-resort lender or deposit insurance institution. Main banking activities occur in various segments, including accepting bank deposits, retail banking, commercial and corporate lending, and corporate finance. The sector is regulated by a supervision model with a separate supervisory entity for each financial market, coordinated within the Financial Coordination Council (CCF). The Superintendency of Banks of Panama is responsible for regulating and supervising various financial entities.

sections.heading: Modernization and Digital Transformation
sections.body:
Experts highlight the need to invest in digitalization, both in customer interactions and internal processes. While some banks have efficient and user-friendly client interfaces, internal operations and processes still require significant improvement. Procedures like loan granting and financial solvency analysis are still slow and rely on archaic mechanisms compared to North American or other Latin American banks.

Nonetheless, the Panamanian financial system has maintained remarkable macroeconomic stability, without any systemic banking crisis attributable to intrinsic imbalances in the banking system. The simultaneous operation of international and local banks allows for significant competitiveness and efficiency. Reflecting its international reach, Panama had 66 banks supervised by the Superintendency of Banks for 4 million inhabitants in 2023. By comparison, using the same criteria and including neobanks, France had 73 banks at the same date.

tax-pressure.title: Moderate Tax Pressure
tax-pressure.subtitle: Tax Efficiency
tax-pressure.shortDescription: Panama's moderate and well-structured tax regime for corporations and individuals makes it particularly attractive to residents, investors, and companies worldwide — built on the principle of territorial taxation.

sections.body:
Panama not only stands out as a place of natural and cultural wonder but also as a country where preferential taxation, financial security, and economic stability prevail. Its moderate and well-structured tax regime for corporations and individuals makes it particularly attractive to residents, investors, and companies worldwide.

Panama's tax system is mainly based on the principle of territoriality, where only income generated on national territory is taxed. This peculiarity has allowed Panama to stand out as an attractive destination for foreign investments.

sections.heading: Direct Taxes Applicable to Corporations
sections.body:
• Income Tax: Equivalent to corporate tax, levied on profits earned by tax-resident companies in Panama. The tax rate is 25%, although it can reach 30% for some public or semi-public entities. There is a minimum effective tax rate for entities with revenues exceeding $1.5 million USD, where the higher of the following two rates applies: either the tax rate on taxable profits or 4.67% of the company's global turnover.

  • The "tasa única" tax: An annual flat tax levied on various entities established in Panama, with an amount of $300 USD, except for private interest foundations, which contribute $350 USD.

  • Resident agent's sworn declaration: Since 2022, lawyers representing companies must file a sworn declaration of the companies' accounts annually. This measure — a consequence of the Panama Papers affair — aims to combat money laundering in the country. This fee of $350 USD is paid by the lawyer and passed on to their client. Although this obligation is not presented as a tax, it is mandatory and paid to the DGI (Dirección General de Impuestos).

  • Complementary Tax: An advance payment of the dividend tax payable by shareholders who receive them. It only applies to entities that distribute less than 40% of their net after-tax profits. The applicable rate is 10% of the difference between the undistributed net profits and 40% of the same net profit.

sections.heading: Direct Taxes Applicable to Individuals
sections.body:
• Income Tax: Panama has a relatively simple, progressive income tax system for individuals: 0% for incomes between $0 and $11,000 USD; 15% for incomes between $11,000 and $50,000 USD (only the portion between $11,000 and $50,000 is taxed); and 25% for incomes over $50,000 USD (taxpayers pay 15% on incomes up to $50,000, and only incomes above $50,000 are taxed at 25%).

  • Dividend Tax: A withholding tax for individuals on shares held in both Panamanian and foreign entities. The rate is 10% for dividends from Panamanian sources and 5% for dividends from foreign sources.

  • Capital Gains Tax: Imposed at a rate of 15% on the profits made from the sale of shares and real estate.

These tax regulations demonstrate Panama's commitment to creating a stable and safe economic environment. The moderation of tax pressure attracts a wide range of investors and companies, thereby enhancing the country's status as a financial hub.

Efficiency and transparency in Panama's tax system have been strengthened over time, especially following the Panama Papers affair. Recent reforms reflect the country's intention to align with international standards while retaining its unique appeal in terms of taxation.

In summary, Panama represents a land of tax opportunities and innovation, where financial stability and security are at the heart of its prosperity. Its clear tax legislation and competitive tax rates make it a preferred destination for entrepreneurs, investors, and individuals seeking growth and asset protection.

articleSections.heading: A Country of Many Landscapes
articleSections.body:
In Panama, distances let you change surroundings without having to cross an enormous territory. Across the country there are Caribbean and Pacific coasts, islands, mangroves, tropical forests, farmland and mountain areas. Each region has its own climate, landscape and character.

Some people prefer urban life, with restaurants, shops, cultural activities and services concentrated in the capital. Others look for a quieter setting, close to the sea or the mountains. Boquete and Tierras Altas attract those who enjoy cooler temperatures and outdoor activities; Bocas del Toro offers an island, Caribbean atmosphere; and various towns in the interior offer a way of life more closely tied to traditions, agriculture and local communities.

Volcán Barú, in Chiriquí province, is the highest point in the country, at 3,475 meters above sea level. In favorable weather, it is possible to see both the Pacific and the Caribbean from its summit. The experience depends on the weather and requires planning, but it illustrates Panama's geographic diversity well: a territory where landscapes can change noticeably from one region to another. MiAMBIENTE describes the volcano's natural setting.

articleSections.heading: Protected Nature and Biodiversity
articleSections.body:
Nature is central to Panamanian identity. The isthmus connects ecosystems of North and South America, and its protected areas span forests, wetlands, coasts, islands and marine spaces. For those who enjoy hiking, birdwatching, diving or simply spending time outdoors, there are very different options depending on the region.

Coiba National Park and its Special Marine Protection Zone, in the Gulf of Chiriquí, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The site comprises Coiba Island, other smaller islands and the surrounding marine areas. Panama also has parks such as Darién, La Amistad, Soberanía and Volcán Barú, each with different landscapes and experiences. Visits to these places must respect conservation rules and the instructions of the environmental authorities.

Living in Panama does not mean everyone will have a beach or a forest a few steps from home. The experience changes a lot depending on the location and the lifestyle you seek. However, the variety of regions lets you compare options before deciding: the activity of the capital, coastal living, the cool climate of the highlands or the tranquility of the interior towns. Even near Panama City you can find natural and cultural spaces, as the domestic tourism offering around the capital shows.

articleSections.heading: A Capital Connected to the World
articleSections.body:
Panama City combines historic neighborhoods, modern residential areas, shops, restaurants and professional services. The Casco Antiguo and Panamá Viejo recall the country's history, while other areas reflect urban growth and contemporary economic activity. It is not a uniform city: each neighborhood has its own atmosphere. That is why, when choosing where to live, it is worth considering factors such as budget, transport, work, schools and proximity to the services you need.

The country's location also eases international travel. Tocumen International Airport is an important regional air connection point. Added to this is the infrastructure linked to the Panama Canal, the ports and the interoceanic railway. This combination has contributed to the development of activities related to services, trade and transport. Panama's logistics network connects maritime, rail and air routes.

For some residents, this connectivity is a practical advantage: it makes it possible to keep ties with other countries, receive visitors and organize work or personal trips. For entrepreneurs and investors, the location can ease relations with markets in Latin America and the Caribbean. The concrete usefulness depends, of course, on each person's activity and mobility needs.

articleSections.heading: A Diverse Society and an Everyday Life of Its Own
articleSections.body:
Panama has a history shaped by the meeting of peoples and cultures. Its ten provinces and six indigenous comarcas reflect a territorial and social diversity that goes beyond the capital. Food, celebrations, music and ways of speaking vary from one region to another.

Many people who move to the country value the chance to integrate into local communities while also finding international groups. However, adapting takes time. Learning how services work, getting familiar with local customs and building personal relationships are part of the moving process. Speaking Spanish makes daily tasks easier and helps you take part more fully in the life of the country.

Hospitality is a common impression among those who visit or settle in Panama, although every experience is personal. As anywhere, a relationship with a community is built on respect, curiosity and participation. Getting to know the surroundings before choosing an area, talking with residents and spending time in different neighborhoods or cities can help you make a more informed decision.

articleSections.heading: The Dollar and Economic Activity
articleSections.body:
Since 1904, the US dollar has circulated legally alongside the balboa, whose parity with the dollar is maintained at one to one. For those arriving from countries that use dollars or who keep income in that currency, this can simplify some aspects of financial planning and everyday payments. Even so, living in Panama means carefully reviewing local expenses, bank fees, each institution's requirements and the tax obligations that apply to your situation. The currency fact is part of the general country information published by PROPANAMA.

Panama's economy is strongly service-oriented, and the country offers different frameworks for business and investment activities. This may interest entrepreneurs, professionals and companies looking to operate in the region. But setting up a company, opening a bank account or investing requires analysis and compliance with requirements; the country's location alone does not guarantee commercial results. The business environment and investment sectors can vary depending on the activity and the applicable regime.

Tax rules must also be analyzed case by case. The Directorate General of Revenue (DGI) explains that income tax can apply to income derived from activities carried out in Panamanian territory, regardless of the beneficiary's nationality, domicile or residence. The DGI details who must pay income tax. For an initial estimate, you can also use our Panama income tax calculator. Each person's tax situation may depend on other factors, including their ties and obligations in other countries; for this reason, verify the applicable rules and get advice before making decisions.

articleSections.heading: Healthcare and Services: Find Out by Area
articleSections.body:
The availability of healthcare services is an important criterion when choosing where to live. Panama has public and private facilities, but the offering, specialties, opening hours and travel times vary by area. Panama City concentrates a significant share of specialized services; in other provinces, the distance to a hospital or clinic may weigh more in daily life.

Before moving, especially if you have specific medical needs, it is advisable to check which centers and services exist near the home you are considering and how to reach them. It is also worth reviewing what coverage your chosen insurance offers and what conditions apply to each person. The Ministry of Health lets you look up available facilities and services.

articleSections.heading: Choosing Panama with Your Eyes Open
articleSections.body:
Moving to Panama can mean starting a new chapter in a connected, diverse and geographically compact country, with landscapes and lifestyles that are very different from each other. For some people, the priority is the professional, urban activity of the capital; for others, it is the climate, nature, closeness to the sea or a quieter life. There is no single Panamanian experience: the best choice depends on the circumstances, expectations and needs of each family or professional.

A well-planned move starts with concrete questions: which city or region do I want to live in? What monthly budget do I need? Which services must I have nearby? What immigration status applies to my case? How will the move affect my banking and tax obligations? Answering them before making decisions helps you compare options realistically and prepare the necessary procedures.

At Panama Contact Services we support those who wish to settle in the country and need guidance on residency, account opening, company formation and other procedures related to their project. Each case requires an individual assessment: we can help you understand the steps, organize the documentation and explore which options fit your plans. Panama offers many possibilities; knowing them well is the first step to deciding whether this is the right place for you.

intro.heading: Are you actually taxable in Panama?
intro.body: Panama only taxes Panamanian-source income. This quiz walks through your residency, income sources, and any Panama company or rental income to estimate your overall tax exposure and flag anything worth a closer look.
intro.territorialBody: Unlike most countries, Panama does not tax based on citizenship or residency alone — it taxes based on where the income is generated. A salary paid by a foreign employer for work performed abroad is exempt, even if you live in Panama full-time. Conversely, income generated inside Panama — from a local company, a local job, or a Panamanian rental property — is taxable even if you live somewhere else entirely.

triggers: Operating a Panama company that invoices Panamanian clients or does business inside the country
Renting out real estate located in Panama
Performing work physically inside Panama, even for a foreign employer
Running a local retail, service, or hospitality business
Having multiple, mixed income streams that combine foreign and Panamanian sources
intro.whyBody: Most people assume moving to Panama means their worldwide income becomes taxable there — it doesn’t. This quiz exists to quickly separate the income that’s actually exposed to Panamanian tax from the income that isn’t, before you dive into exact numbers with the income tax calculator.

faq.question: Am I taxable in Panama if I live abroad?
faq.answer: Panama taxes are based on where income is sourced, not where you live. If you reside abroad but earn Panama-source income — for example from a Panama company or rental property — that income can still be taxable in Panama.

faq.question: What counts as Panama-source income?
faq.answer: Income generated by work performed in Panama, by a Panama-based company operating locally, from renting real estate in Panama, or from professional services rendered within the country.

faq.question: Does owning a Panama company make me taxable?
faq.answer: Not automatically. If your Panama company only generates foreign-source income (for example, invoicing overseas clients for services performed outside Panama), that income is generally exempt. Panama tax applies when the company’s income is generated within Panama.

faq.question: Is rental income in Panama taxable?
faq.answer: Yes. Renting out property located in Panama produces Panama-source income, which is generally subject to income tax regardless of your residency status.

faq.question: How accurate is this quiz?
faq.answer: This quiz is a screening tool that flags your likely level of tax exposure based on your answers. It's a helpful starting point, not a substitute for a full review by a licensed tax professional.

faq.answer: We recommend booking a consultation with our team so a licensed CPA can review your specific structure, confirm your filing obligations, and identify ways to optimize your tax position.

usAlert.heading: You may have U.S. tax obligations too
usAlert.body: As a U.S. citizen or Green Card holder, the IRS taxes your worldwide income regardless of where you live — Panama's territorial tax system doesn't change your U.S. filing obligations. You likely still need to file U.S. tax returns, and possibly FBAR/FATCA disclosures, even if your income is fully exempt in Panama. This requires cross-border tax planning with someone who understands both systems.
